title: Final Accounts and Marshalling of the Balance Sheet
tagline: Capital and revenue treatment, the trading and profit and loss account with adjustments, and the two orderings of a balance sheet.

overview.intro: At the end of an accounting period the ledger balances must be turned into statements a reader can use. The trading account finds the gross profit on a merchandising business, the profit and loss account converts that figure into net profit after overheads and other charges, and the balance sheet shows what the business owns and owes on the closing day. Getting there requires two judgements first: whether an item is capital or revenue, and which adjustment belongs in which statement. This unit covers capital and revenue expenditure, income and losses, provisions and reserves, the three statements with and without adjustments, and marshalling, the deliberate ordering of balance sheet items by permanence or by liquidity.

facts.label: Capital vs revenue
facts.value: Capital items benefit more than one period and go to the balance sheet; revenue items benefit one period and go to the trading or profit and loss account.

facts.label: Trading account
facts.value: Sales less cost of goods sold, where cost = opening stock + purchases + direct expenses − closing stock.

facts.label: Adjustments
facts.value: Outstanding and prepaid expenses, accrued and advance income, depreciation, bad debts and reserve for doubtful debts, closing stock.

facts.label: Marshalling
facts.value: Ordering by permanence, fixed assets first, or by liquidity, the most convertible to cash first.

learningOutcomes: Distinguish capital expenditure, revenue expenditure, capital income and revenue income.
Prepare a trading account and interpret gross profit.
Prepare a profit and loss account and a balance sheet with adjustments.
Apply the rules for provisions and reserves.
Marshal a balance sheet by permanence and by liquidity.

learn.title: Capital and revenue: expenditure, income, receipts

blocks.text: The distinction between capital and revenue decides where an item appears, and therefore whether it affects this year’s profit at all. Capital expenditure is incurred to acquire an asset or to increase the value or earning capacity of an existing asset, and its benefit lasts several years: the cost of a machine, the alteration of a shop front, the first year’s insurance on a new van. Revenue expenditure is incurred to maintain the asset or to run the business for the current period: repairs, wages, rent, electricity. Capital revenue and capital receipts are the other side of the coin, such as the proceeds of a sale of investments or an issue of shares, which are credited to capital and never to the profit and loss account.

items: Ask how long the benefit lasts: one period means revenue, several periods means capital.
Ask whether the item maintains earning capacity or increases it; maintenance is revenue.
Ask whether the item is recurring; annual repairs are revenue even though large.
Capital items never enter the profit and loss account except as depreciation of the asset.

items.text: ₹40,000 spent adding a second floor to a owned shop.
items.note: Capital expenditure: the building’s value and usefulness are increased beyond the current year.

items.text: ₹40,000 spent repainting and rewiring the shop each year.
items.note: Revenue expenditure: the spend maintains the existing earning capacity of an asset already owned.

blocks.text: A provision is a charge against profit created for a known liability or a diminution in the value of an asset, where the amount may be uncertain: provision for doubtful debts, provision for depreciation, provision for taxation. A reserve is an appropriation of profit, not a charge against it, and it strengthens the financial position: general reserve, dividend equalisation reserve, capital redemption reserve. The practical difference appears in the profit and loss account: a provision is debited before arriving at net profit, while a reserve is debited after net profit is found, out of the profit that is available for distribution.

blocks.caption: Provision against reserve
rows: Meet a known liability or fall in asset value
A deliberate decision of the management

blocks.text: A capital reserve is created out of capital profits such as a gain on the reissue of forfeited shares and cannot be distributed as dividend, while a revenue reserve is created out of normal trading profits and can be used for any purpose the Articles permit.

The trading account measures the gross profit of a merchandising business by matching sales against the cost of the goods that were sold. The cost of goods sold is opening stock plus purchases, plus direct expenses such as carriage inwards, freight and wages of the factory, less closing stock. The account is opened with credit sales; if a figure is given as sales including excise or sales returns are shown separately, those must be adjusted first. A credit balance in the account is gross profit transferred to the profit and loss account; a debit balance is gross loss, which happens when the cost of goods sold exceeds sales.

blocks.caption: Trading account for the year ended 31 March (with adjustments)

items: Closing stock appears on the credit side and is simultaneously shown as a current asset.
Direct expenses belong here: carriage inwards, wages of production, factory rent.
Indirect expenses such as office rent and salaries go to the profit and loss account.
Goods withdrawn by the owner for personal use are deducted from purchases.

learn.title: Profit and loss account and balance sheet with adjustments

blocks.text: The profit and loss account starts with gross profit brought down and debits every indirect expense: rent, rates, salaries, advertising, bad debts, discount allowed, depreciation. It credits indirect incomes such as commission and interest received, and the balance is net profit or net loss, which is transferred to capital. The balance sheet is a statement, not an account: assets on one side, liabilities and capital on the other, and the two totals must agree after net profit or loss has been added to or deducted from opening capital.

Five adjustments recur and each appears twice, once in the statement and once in the balance sheet. Outstanding expenses are added to the expense and shown as a liability. Prepaid expenses are deducted from the expense and shown as an asset. Accrued income is added to the income and shown as an asset. Income received in advance is deducted from the income and shown as a liability. Closing stock is credited to the trading account and shown as a current asset. Depreciation and bad debts reduce the asset value and the profit together, and a reserve for doubtful debts is deducted from debtors after bad debts have been removed.

blocks.caption: Where each adjustment appears
rows: Debited to profit and loss account
Debited to profit and loss account

items.text: Rent of ₹60,000 of which ₹10,000 is unpaid at the year end.
items.note: Charge ₹70,000 in the profit and loss account and show ₹10,000 as a liability for outstanding rent.

items.text: Insurance ₹12,000 paid covering twelve months from 1 January, year ending 31 March.
items.note: Three months are prepaid, so charge ₹9,000 and show ₹3,000 as a current asset.

blocks.text: Marshalling is the arrangement of balance sheet items in a deliberate order so that the reader gets the emphasis the statement is meant to convey. Under the permanence method, the most permanent and least liquid items appear first: fixed assets such as land and buildings and machinery, then investments, then current assets, and on the liabilities side share capital and reserves first, then long-term liabilities, then current liabilities. This order stresses the long-term stability of the business. Under the liquidity method the order reverses: cash and bank first on the asset side and creditors and bills payable first on the liability side, because both orders run from the most liquid to the least liquid.

blocks.caption: Ordering by permanence and by liquidity

items: Permanence order runs from least liquid to most liquid, stressing stability.
Liquidity order runs from most liquid to least liquid, stressing near-term solvency.
Both orders must be applied consistently to both sides of the statement.
The basis adopted is disclosed in the notes to the accounts.

items.text: A bank lending short-term working capital wants the liquidity ordering.
items.note: Cash and near-cash assets appear first, showing how quickly obligations can be met.

items.text: A shareholder assessing long-term stability prefers the permanence ordering.
items.note: Fixed assets and capital appear first, showing the durable base of the business.

keyPoints: Capital expenditure benefits more than one period and is shown in the balance sheet.
Revenue expenditure maintains the business for the current period and is charged against profit.
A provision is a charge against profit; a reserve is an appropriation after net profit.
Cost of goods sold = opening stock + purchases + direct expenses − closing stock.
Gross profit is the credit balance of the trading account; a debit balance is gross loss.
Indirect expenses and incomes belong to the profit and loss account, not the trading account.
Every adjustment appears twice: once in a statement and once in the balance sheet.
Net profit increases capital and net loss reduces it before the balance sheet is drawn up.
Marshalling orders items by permanence or by liquidity on both sides.
The basis of ordering chosen for the balance sheet is disclosed in the notes.
examFocus: Adjustment questions are marked on the double effect: an entry in the wrong statement costs marks even if the arithmetic is right.
Show closing stock twice, credited in the trading account and listed as a current asset, because examiners look for exactly this.
In marshalling questions, state the basis first and then give the sequence; an unordered list earns only part marks.

questions.prompt: Carriage paid on goods purchased is shown in:
options: The trading account as a direct expense
The profit and loss account as an indirect expense
The balance sheet as a liability
questions.answer: The trading account as a direct expense
questions.explanation: Carriage inwards brings goods to their present location and condition, so it forms part of the cost of goods sold in the trading account.

options: Only on the credit side of the trading account
Only as a current asset in the balance sheet
Twice: in the trading account and as a current asset
Only in the profit and loss account
questions.answer: Twice: in the trading account and as a current asset
questions.explanation: Every adjustment has a double effect, and closing stock is credited to the trading account while being listed as a current asset.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a reserve and not a provision?
questions.explanation: A general reserve is an appropriation of profit, whereas the other three are charges against profit for a known liability or a fall in asset value.

questions.prompt: In a balance sheet arranged by the liquidity method, the first asset listed is:
questions.explanation: The liquidity method begins with the asset most easily converted into cash, while share capital belongs on the liabilities side.

questions.prompt: The expense incurred to bring purchased goods to their present location and condition, shown in the trading account, is carriage __________ .
questions.explanation: Carriage inwards is a direct expense forming part of the cost of goods sold, while carriage outwards is an indirect expense of the profit and loss account.

questions.prompt: Expenses paid in advance before the year end, and shown as an asset until the benefit is used up, are called __________ expenses.
questions.explanation: They are deducted from the related expense in the profit and loss account and listed as a current asset, because the benefit belongs to the following period.

questions.prompt: State the meaning of capital expenditure and give two examples.
questions.answer: Capital expenditure is expenditure incurred to acquire a new asset or to increase the value or earning capacity of an existing asset, whose benefit extends over more than one accounting period. Two examples are the purchase of machinery for the factory and the cost of adding a second floor to the business premises.
questions.explanation: The definition must include the benefit lasting more than one period; examples alone do not earn the definition marks.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between a provision and a reserve.
questions.answer: A provision is a charge against profit created for a known liability or a diminution in the value of an asset, and it is debited before net profit is arrived at. A reserve is an appropriation of profit created to strengthen the financial position, and it is debited after net profit is found. Examples are a provision for doubtful debts and a general reserve respectively.
questions.explanation: Three points of contrast are expected: nature, purpose and position in the accounts.

questions.prompt: Explain any five adjustments commonly made in the final accounts of a trading concern.
questions.answer: Outstanding expenses are added to the expense and shown as a current liability. Prepaid expenses are deducted from the expense and shown as a current asset. Accrued income is added to the income shown as a current asset, while income received in advance is deducted from the income and shown as a current liability. Closing stock is credited to the trading account and shown as a current asset. Bad debts are debited to the profit and loss account and, along with any reserve for doubtful debts, deducted from debtors in the balance sheet. Depreciation is debited to the profit and loss account and deducted from the asset.
questions.explanation: Full marks require the double effect of each adjustment: where it enters the statement and where it appears in the balance sheet.

questions.prompt: Gross profit is ₹4,20,000. Indirect expenses are: rent ₹60,000 of which ₹10,000 is outstanding, salaries ₹1,20,000 of which ₹15,000 is prepaid, depreciation ₹40,000 and bad debts ₹5,000. Indirect income is interest received ₹8,000 of which ₹2,000 is accrued. Find the net profit.
questions.answer: Net profit is ₹2,10,000. Rent charged is 60,000 + 10,000 = ₹70,000 with ₹10,000 shown as a liability; salaries charged are 1,20,000 − 15,000 = ₹1,05,000 with ₹15,000 shown as a prepaid asset; depreciation ₹40,000 and bad debts ₹5,000 are charged in full. Interest received is 8,000 + 2,000 = ₹10,000 with ₹2,000 shown as an accrued asset. Net profit = 4,20,000 + 10,000 − 70,000 − 1,05,000 − 40,000 − 5,000 = ₹2,10,000.
questions.explanation: Every adjustment must be applied in the direction the year-end position demands: add the unpaid rent and the unrecorded interest, remove the prepaid salaries, and the balance must then actually total ₹3,03,000.
